title: The Seamstress in the Royalist Houses: Guaduas, the Reconquista, and the Plaza Mayor
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Guaduas, the birth on the royal road
stops.date_confidence: canonical but not settled: es.wikipedia gives 26 January 1795, other encyclopedic accounts 1796, Banrepcultural a range of 1793-1795
stops.campa: In the villa of San Miguel de Guaduas, on the royal road between Santafé and the Magdalena port of Honda, Joaquín Salavarrieta and Mariana Ríos have a daughter. The parish gives her Policarpa; the century will give her La Pola. Three towns claim the birth, Guaduas, Bogotá and Mariquita, and the Colombian Academy of History does not affirm Guaduas until the tenth of September, 1991. An academy voted on the birthplace of a national heroine, which is not the same thing as a document. The road she is born beside is the road the king's army will come up.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of San Miguel de Guaduas, Cundinamarca
The Colombian Academy of History ruling of 10 September 1991 on her birthplace

stops.name: Santa Bárbara, the family comes down to the capital
stops.date_confidence: contested year: es.wikipedia gives 1797, biografiasyvidas.com 1798; month defaulted to January
stops.campa: The family leaves the mule road and comes down into Santafé de Bogotá, taking a house of adobe and tile in the parish of Santa Bárbara, between the sixth and seventh streets. Her father has business enough to move a household of eight down off the road. The capital of the viceroyalty is a town of clerics, oidores and muleteers, and the parish bell measures the day. Policarpa is two years old, or three, and will remember none of it. She is now a child of the city she will be shot in.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de Santa Bárbara, Carrera 7 with Calle 6a, and its colonial parish limits

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the smallpox year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1802; en.wikipedia places the deaths in August and September, so the month is that source's and the day is defaulted
stops.campa: Smallpox comes over the sabana in August and does not leave until the rains. Joaquín Salavarrieta dies; Mariana Ríos dies; two of the children die with them, a sister called María Ignacia and a brother whom Spanish Wikipedia names Joaquín and English Wikipedia names Eduardo. The house in Santa Bárbara is broken up and the surviving children are handed out among relatives. A year before, Alexander von Humboldt sat two months in this same city over the herbarium of José Celestino Mutis. Policarpa is seven years old and has no parents.
suggested_refs: Parish burial records of Santa Bárbara for the 1802 epidemic
Humboldt's Bogotá sojourn of July 1801 with the Royal Botanical Expedition

stops.name: Guaduas, the godmother's house
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the sources say circa 1804 and fix nothing closer; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her elder sister Catalina takes Policarpa and their brother Bibiano back up the road to Guaduas, to the house of the godmother Margarita Beltrán and an aunt called Manuela. The orphan grows into the trade that will carry her everywhere: needle, thread, and the right to sit in another woman's front room for an entire afternoon. She is nine years old. In a viceregal town the seamstress is the one visitor no household questions, and no household remembers afterward.
suggested_refs: The house of Margarita Beltrán at Guaduas, godmother's household of the orphaned Salavarrieta children

stops.name: Guaduas, the Convento de la Soledad
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no document places her in the convent, and no year is given by any source; the date is a placeholder inside the Guaduas adolescence
stops.campa: Local tradition sets her at the Convento de la Soledad, learning letters among the nuns, and some accounts have her teaching reading afterward in a public school. Spanish Wikipedia flags the teaching claim itself as tradition rather than record, and no primary document places her in the convent as pupil or as mistress. What is certain is that she reads and writes, which in a town this size is already a small office. The lists she will carry in 1817 are lists she can read.
suggested_refs: The Convento de la Soledad at Guaduas, named by local tradition as her school

stops.name: Guaduas, Alejo Sabaraín
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a single biographical page gives about 1809, uncorroborated in this pass; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The brothers Leandro and Alejo Sabaraín come into her circle in Guaduas, and Alejo becomes her betrothed. The reconstruction of her last year runs entirely through him: his commission, his journey east, his capture, the paper he is carrying when they take him. The date rests on one biographical page and is corroborated nowhere else. They are young in a town on the road that carries every piece of news from the capital down toward the river. The next piece of news to come up it is that the criollos have broken with the viceroy.
suggested_refs: The Sabaraín family of Guaduas, and the betrothal that ends at the same firing squad

stops.name: Guaduas, the news of the twentieth of July
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: biografiasyvidas.com dates her learning of it to 22 July 1810 and does not explain the two-day lag from the act of 20 July
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July the criollos of Santafé break with the viceroy over a borrowed flower vase and a crowd in the plaza. The news walks the road to Guaduas and arrives, one source says, on the twenty-second. The town takes the fever. Policarpa is fifteen, and everything she will be arrested for eight years later is in Guaduas that week ordinary conversation among her brothers and her betrothed. Nobody in the town is yet doing anything a royalist tribunal would call treason.
suggested_refs: The Acta de Independencia of Santafé, 20 July 1810, and its transmission along the Honda road

stops.name: La Candelaria, the household of María Matea Martínez de Zaldúa
stops.date_confidence: single-source and contradicted: only biografiasyvidas.com carries this employment, and the same page elsewhere has her arriving in the capital for the first time in 1817
stops.campa: She comes down to Santafé and takes work in the household of María Matea Martínez de Zaldúa as nursemaid and seamstress, from January of 1812. One biographical page carries this; a full-text scan finds the name nowhere in Spanish Wikipedia, which dates her involvement from 1816. Either she is a resident of this city from 1812 or she arrives in 1817 with forged papers, and both readings come off the same page. The address is not documented, so the pin sits on the Candelaria and not on a door.
suggested_refs: The Martínez de Zaldúa household of the Candelaria, her first documented employer in the capital

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the patriots fight each other at San Victorino
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle; her presence in the city depends on the contested 1812 employment
stops.campa: The two armies that meet at Santafé in January are both patriot. Antonio Nariño's centralist Estado Libre de Cundinamarca holds the city, the federalist Provincias Unidas march on it under Baraya, and on the ninth of January the centralists break them at San Victorino: six hundred federalist dead, twelve hundred and thirty-five taken. The republic is thirty months old and already shooting at itself. Any account that calls this a defence of the city against an attacker has invented a royalist.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of San Victorino, 9 January 1813, at the western edge of colonial Santafé

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, Sabaraín arrives with the fever
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: biografiasyvidas.com places the tabardillo in February 1813, contracted on arrival; a June date circulating in working drafts has no basis in the source
stops.campa: Alejo Sabaraín reaches Santafé as a subteniente in the patriot forces and falls sick on arrival with tabardillo, the fever that empties barracks faster than any enemy. Biographers put Policarpa in the city through his illness; nothing puts her at the bedside, and the fever itself is carried by one page only, which puts it in February, while the June date in circulation has no basis in that page at all. He recovers. The war finds work for him before the year is out, and the work takes him south.
suggested_refs: Military hospital records of Santafé for the tabardillo outbreak of 1813

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the Campaña del Sur marches out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: single-source date from biografiasyvidas.com
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of September the Campaña del Sur marches out of Santafé toward Popayán and Pasto, Nariño at its head and Sabaraín somewhere in the column. The campaign will end in disaster at the Ejido de Pasto and in Nariño's long captivity in Cádiz. What it does to Policarpa is simpler and goes unrecorded: it takes her betrothed out of the city and leaves a seamstress with no property in a capital that will belong to the king again within three years.
suggested_refs: Nariño's Campaña del Sur, 1813-1814, and its muster rolls

stops.name: Guaduas, the return before the reconquest
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: one biographical page, no document, month approximate
stops.campa: She goes back up to Guaduas before the year closes, out of the capital and into the town where she is known, and the needle sustains her. The reconstruction here is thin and rests on a single page. What is not thin is the direction the war is taking: Cartagena will hold and then fall, the Spanish will come up the Magdalena, and the road through Guaduas is the road they will use. She is eighteen and living at the hinge of it, sewing for a town that has two years left of thinking itself free.
suggested_refs: The Honda-Santafé royal road through Guaduas, the invasion route of 1816

stops.name: Guaduas, the king's officers come up the road
stops.date_confidence: corrected and reconstructed: working drafts said 1815, which is impossible, since Cartagena capitulated 6 December 1815 and Morillo moved inland only in February 1816; month approximate
stops.campa: Morillo's expeditionary army finishes with Cartagena on the sixth of December, 1815, and starts inland in February. Cachirí falls on the twenty-second of February and the news reaches Santafé on the fifth of March. Guaduas, on the Honda road, goes over to the king in that year; the accounts that date the occupation to 1815 put it a whole campaign season early. Policarpa is living in the town when the king's officers ride into it, and she is not yet anybody the king's officers have reason to know.
suggested_refs: The Reconquista of New Granada, 1815-1816, and Morillo's march from the Magdalena

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, Morillo and the Régimen del Terror
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1816; day defaulted
stops.campa: Morillo enters Santafé in May and installs the machinery of the reconquest: the Consejo de Guerra Permanente, the Junta de Secuestros, the Tribunal de Purificación. Camilo Torres is shot, Francisco José de Caldas is shot, the generation that made the first republic is killed off in a season. Antonio José de Sucre had defended Cartagena against this same armada the year before and got out. The tribunal that will try Policarpa is now sitting, eighteen months before it hears her name.
suggested_refs: The Consejo de Guerra Permanente of Santafé, tribunal of the Régimen del Terror

stops.name: Pore, Casanare, the war moves to the plains
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Casanare base is attested for the period, the month is a placeholder and no source traces the routes
stops.campa: What the reconquest cannot reach is the plain. Patriots driven off the cordillera regroup in the Llanos with Pore for a capital, and the war continues there as cattle, horses and horsemen. The Bogotá networks feed it recruits, walking them east over the páramo in twos and threes. In the same years, on the far side of the continent, Juana Azurduy holds the republiqueta of La Laguna against the same empire. No document connects the two women. The empire connects them.
suggested_refs: Pore, Casanare, seat of the patriot resistance in the Llanos, 1816-1819

stops.name: Guaduas, the colonel's proposal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the officer, the meeting and the month all come from one biographical page and are uncorroborated
stops.campa: A patriot officer remembered only as Coronel Rodríguez comes to her in Guaduas and asks her to carry intelligence into the capital. She accepts. The name, the meeting and the month come from a single page and should be held loosely; the office she accepts is real enough. A woman who sews can enter any house in Santafé, and no sentry in the history of the viceroyalty has been posted against a needle. She is twenty-one years old, and nobody writes down what she says when she says yes.
suggested_refs: The unidentified Coronel Rodríguez, named by tradition as her recruiter

segments.name: The Seamstress in the Royalist Houses

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, arrival with false papers
stops.date_confidence: single-source and in tension with the 1812 arrival on the same page; day defaulted
stops.campa: In January she comes down to Santafé with her brother Bibiano and a forged safe-conduct, presenting herself as a seamstress looking for work. This stands against the claim on the same page that she has lived in the city since 1812, and both accounts survive without one displacing the other. The false passport is the only document of her espionage that any source describes as surviving. She leaves no letters, no diary, and no portrait taken from life; every face of her that Colombia knows was invented after her death.
suggested_refs: The forged safe-conduct of 1817, the only document of her espionage said to survive

stops.name: Casa de Andrea Ricaurte de Lozano, the front room that runs a war
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1817; the month is a placeholder within the year
stops.campa: She lodges in the house of Andrea Ricaurte de Lozano, and the house is the operation. Messages come in from the Llanos and go back out to them, recruits are found and fitted out and walked east, money and powder are moved. María del Carmen Rodríguez de Obregón works the same network. It is a war run by women out of a front room, in a city where every royalist officer has his coat mended by somebody. The guerrillas of Casanare are being fed from a sewing basket.
suggested_refs: The house of Andrea Ricaurte de Lozano in the Candelaria, operational center of the network

stops.name: Barrio Egipto, the corner of the Calvario and San Bruno
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: single-source address with no document, pin approximate to the block; month a placeholder
stops.campa: On the eastern edge of the city, where the streets run up against the mountain, a second address serves the network: the corner of the calle del Calvario and the carrera de San Bruno, in the barrio of Egipto. Messages and men are said to pass through it. One biographical page gives the corner and no document supports it, so the pin marks a block and not a house. Above it the trail to the páramo begins, and the páramo is the road to the plains. Men leave the city that way, in twos, at night.
suggested_refs: The barrio Egipto and the old trail east over the páramo toward the Llanos

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the lists and the recruits
stops.date_confidence: attested method, undated: es.wikipedia describes the espionage without fixing months; the date is a placeholder mid-year
stops.campa: She sews in royalist houses and listens: troop numbers, the movement of the correo, which officers are venal and which are frightened. Through intermediaries she helps buy arms and war material, and she turns young men toward the Llanos. She keeps lists of royalists and of patriots, and one of those lists she gives to Alejo Sabaraín. Nobody in this city writes down what a seamstress sees, which is exactly why she can see it. The list is the only thing she puts in writing that outlives her.
suggested_refs: The list of royalist and patriot names carried by Alejo Sabaraín

stops.name: The eastern trail, Sabaraín sets out for the Llanos
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: early August per one biographical page; the route is a corridor, not a point, and the pin marks the corridor
stops.campa: In August Sabaraín leaves Santafé for the Llanos by the mountain trail east of the city, over the páramo and down. He carries the list she gave him. The páramo is a day of wet grass and cold above the tree line before the ground falls away toward the plain, and every courier the network has sent this way has come through it. He is a subteniente carrying a woman's handwriting through royalist country, and he has made the crossing before. He is the one who does not come through.
suggested_refs: The colonial trail from Santafé east over the páramo toward Casanare

stops.name: The road toward Casanare, the capture of Alejo Sabaraín
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date is single-source and the site is fixed by no source; the coordinate is an approximation along the known corridor
stops.campa: On the third of September a royalist patrol takes Sabaraín and his companions somewhere on the eastern road. No source fixes the place. In his baggage is the list of names, in a hand that can be walked back to a house in the Candelaria. From this moment the network in Santafé is a set of names on a piece of paper in the hands of the Consejo de Guerra Permanente, and what follows is arithmetic. Nine people will be shot because of a document in a saddlebag on a mountain road.
suggested_refs: The royalist patrol reports of September 1817 on the Casanare road

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the Almeida brothers are taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1817 only: no source read fixes the sequence against Sabaraín's capture, so the month here is inferred
stops.campa: The brothers Ambrosio and Vicente Almeida are taken carrying documents that compromise her by name. The tribunals of the reconquest now hold two independent papers pointing at the same seamstress. The order of the two captures is fixed by nothing read in this pass, and no source names the day either. What the papers establish is not that she carried messages but that she is the one the messages were for. The house in the Candelaria has about three weeks left.
suggested_refs: The Almeida brothers of Santafé and the documents taken with them

stops.name: A few blocks south of the Ricaurte house, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: contested: biografiasyvidas.com dates the arrest to the night of 10 November, while es.wikipedia, en.wikipedia and Banrepcultural give 10 November as the date of sentence; the conflict is printed, not resolved
stops.campa: They come for her at Andrea Ricaurte's house and she runs. Spanish Wikipedia has her seized only a few blocks south, in the street, so the pin sits there and not on the door she went out of. Her brother Bibiano is taken with her. One source dates the arrest to the night of the tenth of November; three others give the tenth of November as the date of her sentence, and the same day cannot be both. Both dates stand in the sources exactly as given, one attached to the arrest and one to the sentence, and nothing here decides between them.
suggested_refs: The streets south of the Ricaurte house in the Candelaria, site of her seizure

segments.name: The Rosario and the Plaza Mayor

stops.name: Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, the cloister as prison
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1817; the day is placed between the arrest and the execution and is not itself documented
stops.campa: The colonial university of Nuestra Señora del Rosario, its cloister requisitioned, holds her in a cell while the tribunal reads the papers. The building is a library, a lecture hall and a prison in the same week, and the men who taught in it were shot the year before. She is twenty-two years old and names nobody. Nothing she says in that cell is written down by anyone who was in the cell; what survives is what guards remembered afterward, which is not the same thing.
suggested_refs: The Claustro of the Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, Calle 12c #6-25, used as a prison in 1817

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the Consejo de Guerra condemns nine
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia, en.wikipedia and Banrepcultural; one source instead assigns this date to her arrest
stops.campa: The Consejo de Guerra condemns nine to be shot: Policarpa Salavarrieta, Alejo Sabaraín Ramos, José María Arcos, Francisco Arellano, José Manuel Díaz, Manuel Salvador Díaz, Antonio Galeano, Esteban Marufu and José María Suárez. Counts of six and of eight companions circulate; the name list gives seven. The sentence is dated four days before it is carried out. Viceroy Juan de Sámano presides over the machine that issues it, and in two years Sámano will leave this city on horseback ahead of Bolívar's army.
suggested_refs: The sentence of the Consejo de Guerra Permanente, 10 November 1817, Archivo General de la Nación

stops.name: Iglesia del Nazareno, the wine refused
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the church is named by one source without procedural detail, and the night before the execution is inferred from the execution date
stops.campa: The church of El Nazareno is named among the sites of her last imprisonment, possibly where the condemned are given the last rites, and the source lists it without saying more. A guard offers her wine. She refuses it in a sentence the Spanish account preserves and the English account renders without its exclamation marks. What she says she will not take from her enemies is not the wine but a glass of water. In the morning she is to be shot in the square she has crossed every day for ten months.
stops.quote: ¡No aceptaría ni un vaso de agua de mis enemigos!
stops.quote_source: es.wikipedia, 'Policarpa Salavarrieta', reporting the night before the execution; no primary citation given on the page
suggested_refs: The Iglesia del Nazareno, Santafé de Bogotá, named among the sites of her final imprisonment

stops.name: Plaza Mayor, nine in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia gives nine in the morning on Friday 14 November 1817, corroborated by en.wikipedia and Banrepcultural, and the date was indeed a Friday
stops.campa: At nine in the morning on Friday the fourteenth of November they are brought into the Plaza Mayor. The bench for traitors faces away from the firing party; she refuses to kneel and refuses to be shot in the back, and is shot facing them. Eight men die with her, Sabaraín among them. This is the ground on which the viceroyalty proclaims its edicts, and it is the ground on which the republic will raise its Bolívar and rename the square after him. She has been in the city ten months.
stops.quote: ¡Pueblo indolente! ¡Cuán distinta sería hoy vuestra suerte si conocierais el precio de la libertad!
stops.quote_source: es.wikipedia, 'Policarpa Salavarrieta', section 'Juicio y muerte', reproducing the traditional text of the scaffold speech; the article cites no primary document for it
suggested_refs: The Plaza Mayor of Santafé, today the Plaza de Bolívar, site of the executions of 14 November 1817

stops.name: Plaza Mayor, the words that do not agree
stops.date_confidence: the event is attested; the text of the speech is tradition, textually attested in secondary literature and verified against no primary source
stops.campa: Four texts of her scaffold speech circulate and no two agree. Spanish Wikipedia opens with the cry to the indolent people; English Wikipedia opens with the order to the soldiers and closes with a line the Spanish text does not carry; literato.es reads diversa for distinta and conocieseis for conocierais; biografiasyvidas.com drops the word aunque. One clause, no olvidéis este ejemplo, could not be relocated in any page read whole. Not one of them cites a trial record, a gazette or an eyewitness.
stops.quote: Viles soldados, volved las armas a los enemigos de vuestra patria.
stops.quote_source: en.wikipedia, 'Policarpa Salavarrieta', section 'Trial and death'; the same speech appears in es.wikipedia, biografiasyvidas.com and literato.es in mutually incompatible wordings
suggested_refs: The four incompatible texts of the scaffold speech, none traced to a primary document

stops.name: Iglesia de la Veracruz, the contested common grave
stops.date_confidence: single-source and contested: only es.wikipedia carries this stage, and en.wikipedia and Banrepcultural have the brothers claim the body directly
stops.campa: Spanish Wikipedia takes her body from the square to a common grave at the church of the Vera Cruz, on the old calle del Arco, the church that Colombia will come to call the pantheon of the martyrs of independence. English Wikipedia and the Banco de la República know nothing of this stage and have her priest brothers claim her directly. The two accounts are printed here side by side. The pin is where the church is, at the seventh carrera with the sixteenth street.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de la Veracruz, Carrera 7 with Calle 16, pantheon of the martyrs of independence

stops.name: Iglesia de San Agustín, the brothers claim her
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, undated: no source gives the day, so the day after the execution is used as a placeholder
stops.campa: Her brothers, both priests, claim the body and carry it to the convent church of San Agustín, behind what will one day be the presidential palace. Banrepcultural adds that unlike her companions she is not left exposed in the streets. She is buried, and then the record stops: Spanish Wikipedia states outright that where her remains now lie is not established. The most reproduced woman in Colombian iconography has no grave to visit. The epitaph that survives is not hers but a fellow prisoner's.
stops.quote_source: Joaquín Monsalve, fellow prisoner, composed for her in prison, per biografiasyvidas.com, 'Policarpa Salavarrieta'
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de San Agustín, Carrera 7 with Calle 7, La Candelaria, her recorded burial place

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the empty palace
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Twenty-one months after the volley in the square, Simón Bolívar comes down from Boyacá and rides into a Santafé whose viceroy has fled and whose palace stands empty. Sámano, who presided over the tribunal that sentenced her, is running for the coast. The city that executed Policarpa and the martyrs of the reconquest receives the Liberator with delirium. Francisco de Paula Santander, in the field with the army in 1817 and nowhere near her trial, is left to govern the country she died for.
suggested_refs: The viceregal palace of Santafé, abandoned by Sámano in August 1819

stops.name: Piura, the Liberty statue with her face
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1870; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In Piura, on the dry coast of northern Peru, the resident Colombian colony inaugurates a statue of Liberty bearing her face, under the government of José Balta. Fifty-three years after the square and a thousand miles from it, she is already a figure rather than a woman: the monument is of Liberty, and the face it wears is hers. Spanish Wikipedia gives the monument no title, and the name Alegoría de la Libertad attached to it elsewhere is not in the source and is not used here.
suggested_refs: The Liberty statue of Piura, 1870, raised by the Colombian colony under José Balta

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a street called Pola
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: By municipal ordinance of the twenty-seventh of November a street in Buenos Aires is named Pola, and Argentine and Uruguayan poets and playwrights take her for a subject, decades after the firing squad that made her one. The continent is sorting its independence heroines into a shared pantheon. She left no letters and no portrait taken from life, so the plays and poems build their heroine on that silence, the same silence that already forced every face of her that Colombia knows into invention after her death.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires municipal ordinance of 27 November 1893 naming the calle Pola

stops.name: Las Aguas, the Dionisio Cortés statue and the centennial stamp
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1910 by both wikis; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: For the centennial of the twentieth of July, Dionisio Cortés raises her statue at the corner of carrera 2A and calle 18, in Las Aguas under the mountain, and the post office puts her on a one-centavo stamp among the heroes. The Enlightenment texts her generation read in manuscript, Rousseau above all, are school property by now. Ninety-three years after the square, the state that shot her is gone and the state that replaced it franks its letters with her.
suggested_refs: Dionisio Cortés, statue of Policarpa Salavarrieta, Carrera 2A with Calle 18, Bogotá, 1910

stops.name: Bogotá, the beer named after her
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1911; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Bavaria brewery launches a beer called La Pola in her honour, and the word takes. A century later a Colombian ordering a pola is ordering a beer and not invoking a martyr, and the etymology is invisible to the person paying for it. A punk band will call itself Policarpa y sus Viciosas. In 2022 a tarantula, Pamphobeteus lapola, is named for her. National mythology does not stay in the pantheon. It gets into the language and orders a drink at the counter.
suggested_refs: Bavaria brewery advertising for La Pola, from 1911

stops.name: Guaduas, the Casa Museo
stops.date_confidence: undated: the sources give only twentieth century, so the year here is a mid-century placeholder carrying no evidentiary weight, and the stop is ordered inside the century rather than at the end of the file
stops.campa: In Guaduas a house identified with her family becomes the Casa Museo Policarpa Salavarrieta, and the town that had to be certified as her birthplace by an academy in 1991 receives the pilgrims. The chain of title back to the colonial period is not documented; the identification rests on local memory, which is what identified the birthplace too. She has no grave, so the country keeps a house instead. The year the museum was founded is fixed in nothing read here.
suggested_refs: The Casa Museo Policarpa Salavarrieta, Guaduas, Cundinamarca

stops.name: Bogotá, Ley 44 and the fourteenth of November
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia to 9 November 1967; en.wikipedia gives the law itself as 14 November, conflating the law with the day it designates
stops.campa: Law 44, signed by President Carlos Lleras Restrepo on the ninth of November, sets the fourteenth of November, the anniversary of her execution, as the Día de la Mujer Colombiana. The law's own date and the date it names are five days apart, and sources conflate them routinely. A republic dates its women's day from a firing squad, and nobody in the chamber puts it that way. The volley the date commemorates killed nine people, and she is the one the calendar names.
suggested_refs: Ley 44 de 1967, Congreso de la República de Colombia

stops.name: Bogotá, her face on the money three times
stops.date_confidence: attested: the ten-thousand-peso note is issued 1 March 1995; the 1972 note and the 1980-1988 coin are dated in the campa, and the coin attribution rests on a single article
stops.campa: She has been on the money three times: a two-peso note issued on the first of January, 1972, purple, with the Muisca raft on the reverse; a five-peso coin struck from 1980 to 1988; and the ten-thousand-peso note issued on the first of March, 1995, with the plaza of Guaduas behind her. In 2016 the anthropologist Virginia Gutiérrez de Pineda takes her place on the ten thousand. The coin attribution rests on one encyclopedia article and is corroborated by nothing else read here.
suggested_refs: The 10,000-peso note of 1 March 1995, reverse showing the plaza of Guaduas

stops.name: Bogotá, La Pola in prime time
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiered 13 September 2010 and ended 27 July 2011, per es.wikipedia; working drafts dated the run to 2010 alone
stops.campa: RCN broadcasts La Pola, ninety-eight episodes directed by Sergio Cabrera, with Carolina Ramírez as the woman and Ana María Estupiñán as the girl, from the thirteenth of September, 2010 to the twenty-seventh of July, 2011. The bicentennial gets its heroine in prime time. The trial documents in the Archivo General de la Nación have still not been read by anybody writing about her in this pass. The archive stays shut. The country learns her off the screen.
suggested_refs: La Pola, RCN Televisión, 98 episodes, 2010-2011, directed by Sergio Cabrera

stops.name: Bogotá, the bicentennial coin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Banco de la República releases a commemorative coin bearing her image. Two hundred and six years after the square, the bank of the republic mints the face of a woman whose entire documented estate was a false passport, a list of names and a needle. Encyclopaedia Britannica's page on her returns a 403 to anyone trying to read it from here, and the bank's own cultural encyclopedia has to be reached by a side door because the main host answers with a bot challenge. The coin is easier to obtain than the sources.
suggested_refs: The Banco de la República bicentennial commemorative coin of 10 January 2023
